cards.title: Control Plane vs Worker Node Components
cards.question: Explain Control Plane vs Worker Node Components
cards.answer_30s: The Control Plane manages cluster state: API Server (REST gateway), etcd (distributed key-value store for cluster state), Scheduler (assigns Pods to nodes), and Controller Manager (reconciliation loops). Worker nodes run kubelet (node agent), kube-proxy (Service networking), and a CRI container runtime (containerd).

code.body:
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'
kubectl get nodes -o wide

cards.typical_use: Explaining how Kubernetes declarative reconciliation works end-to-end.
pitfalls: Every component talks only to the API Server—nothing talks directly to etcd except the API Server.

cards.title: Pods, ReplicaSets, Deployments & DaemonSets
cards.question: Explain Pods, ReplicaSets, Deployments & DaemonSets
cards.answer_30s: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit (1+ tightly coupled containers sharing network/IPC namespaces). ReplicaSets maintain N identical Pods; Deployments manage ReplicaSets for declarative rolling updates and rollbacks; DaemonSets run one Pod per node (e.g. log/metric agents).

code.body:
kubectl rollout status deployment/api-server
kubectl rollout undo deployment/api-server

cards.typical_use: Managing stateless services and zero-downtime releases.
pitfalls: Never deploy bare Pods in production—always wrap them in Deployments, StatefulSets, or Jobs.

cards.title: Services (ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer) & Ingress
cards.question: Explain Services (ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer) & Ingress
cards.answer_30s: Pod IPs are ephemeral. Services provide a stable virtual IP and DNS name (`svc.ns.svc.cluster.local`) load-balanced across matching Pod labels. ClusterIP is internal-only; NodePort exposes a port on every node; LoadBalancer provisions a cloud LB; Ingress/Gateway API routes L7 HTTP host/path traffic.

code.body:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api-svc
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: api
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8000

cards.typical_use: Exposing internal microservices and routing external HTTPS traffic.
pitfalls: Know that kube-proxy programs iptables/IPVS rules on nodes to route ClusterIP traffic to healthy Endpoints/EndpointSlices.

cards.title: Startup, Readiness & Liveness Probes
cards.question: Explain Startup, Readiness & Liveness Probes
cards.answer_30s: Startup probes wait for slow-booting apps before activating other probes. Readiness probes control whether a Pod receives Service traffic (removes Pod from Endpoints on failure). Liveness probes restart a deadlocked container.

code.body:
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /health/ready
    port: 8000
  periodSeconds: 5
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /health/live
    port: 8000
  failureThreshold: 3

cards.typical_use: Preventing traffic from hitting initializing or overloaded Pods.
pitfalls: Never include external DB checks inside a livenessProbe—if the DB blips, Kubernetes will restart all your API Pods simultaneously!

cards.title: Resource Requests, Limits, QoS & HPA
cards.question: Explain Resource Requests, Limits, QoS & HPA
cards.answer_30s: Requests reserve CPU/memory for kube-scheduler placement; Limits cap cgroup usage (CPU gets throttled; exceeding memory triggers OOMKill). Equal requests and limits yield `Guaranteed` QoS (last to be evicted). HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA) scales replicas on CPU/custom metrics.

code.body:
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "250m"
    memory: "256Mi"
  limits:
    cpu: "1000m"
    memory: "512Mi"

cards.typical_use: Preventing noisy-neighbor starvation and autoscaling under traffic spikes.
pitfalls: Many teams omit CPU limits (keeping CPU requests) to avoid CFS throttling while strictly enforcing memory limits.

cards.title: RBAC, Pod Security & NetworkPolicies
cards.question: Explain RBAC, Pod Security & NetworkPolicies
cards.answer_30s: RBAC restricts API actions via Role/ClusterRole and RoleBinding. Pod Security Standards enforce `runAsNonRoot`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem`, and `drop: [ALL]` capabilities. NetworkPolicies act as L3/L4 firewalls restricting Pod-to-Pod ingress/egress.

code.body:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: db-allow-api
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app: postgres }
  ingress:
    - from: [{ podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: api } } }]

cards.typical_use: Enforcing zero-trust lateral movement boundaries inside multi-tenant clusters.
pitfalls: Remember Kubernetes Secrets are base64-encoded by default, not encrypted—enable etcd encryption at rest or use External Secrets Operator.

cards.title: StatefulSets, Headless Services & PersistentVolumeClaims
cards.question: Explain StatefulSets, Headless Services & PersistentVolumeClaims
cards.answer_30s: StatefulSets give Pods stable network identities (`db-0`, `db-1`), ordered deployment/scaling, and dedicated PersistentVolumeClaims (PVCs) that survive Pod rescheduling—ideal for databases and Kafka.

code.body:
spec:
  serviceName: "postgres-headless"
  replicas: 3
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata: { name: data }
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        resources: { requests: { storage: 50Gi } }

cards.typical_use: Running stateful distributed systems cleanly on Kubernetes.
pitfalls: A Headless Service (`clusterIP: None`) returns individual Pod IPs via DNS instead of load-balancing behind a single VIP.

cards.title: Rolling Updates, Graceful Shutdown & PodDisruptionBudgets
cards.question: Explain Rolling Updates, Graceful Shutdown & PodDisruptionBudgets
cards.answer_30s: Deployments control rollout velocity with `maxSurge` and `maxUnavailable`. PodDisruptionBudgets (PDBs) guarantee a minimum number of available Pods during voluntary node drains. Pair `preStop` sleep hooks with SIGTERM handling so kube-proxy removes the Pod before the app stops accepting requests.
cards.typical_use: Achieving zero dropped requests during deployments and node upgrades.
pitfalls: A short `preStop` sleep solves the async race between Endpoint removal and SIGTERM delivery.

cards.title: Q: How do you troubleshoot a Pod stuck in Pending, ImagePullBackOff, or CrashLoopBackOff?
cards.question: Q: How do you troubleshoot a Pod stuck in Pending, ImagePullBackOff, or CrashLoopBackOff?
cards.answer_30s: A: Run `kubectl describe pod <name>` to read Events first. `Pending` means insufficient CPU/RAM, node taints, or unbound PVCs. `ImagePullBackOff` means wrong image tag, private registry auth missing (`imagePullSecrets`), or network block. `CrashLoopBackOff` means the app starts and exits—check `kubectl logs <name> --previous` and exit codes (137 = OOMKilled).
cards.typical_use: Most common Kubernetes operational troubleshooting question.
pitfalls: Always mention `--previous` for CrashLoopBackOff to see the logs from the crashed container.

cards.title: Q: What happens step by step when `kubectl apply` creates a Deployment?
cards.question: Q: What happens step by step when `kubectl apply` creates a Deployment?
cards.answer_30s: A: kubectl sends the manifest to the API Server -> AuthN/AuthZ/Admission Controllers validate/mutate it -> API Server persists it to etcd -> Deployment Controller creates a ReplicaSet -> ReplicaSet Controller creates Pod objects -> Scheduler binds each Pod to a Node -> Kubelet on that node pulls images via CRI, sets up CNI networking, mounts volumes, and starts containers.
cards.typical_use: Demonstrating mastery of Kubernetes control-loop architecture.
pitfalls: Highlight that controllers follow a level-triggered reconciliation loop (compare desired state vs actual state).

cards.title: Q: Deployment vs StatefulSet vs DaemonSet vs Job — when do you use each?
cards.question: Q: Deployment vs StatefulSet vs DaemonSet vs Job — when do you use each?
cards.answer_30s: A: Deployment for stateless interchangeable web/API Pods. StatefulSet for stateful workloads needing stable hostnames, ordered startup, and persistent per-Pod storage. DaemonSet for node-level infrastructure agents (FluentBit, Prometheus node-exporter). Job/CronJob for finite batch tasks that run to completion.
pitfalls: Mention `ttlSecondsAfterFinished` on Jobs to clean up completed Pod clutter automatically.

cards.title: Q: How do Taints/Tolerations differ from Node Affinity?
cards.question: Q: How do Taints/Tolerations differ from Node Affinity?
cards.answer_30s: A: Taints live on Nodes and repel Pods unless the Pod has a matching Toleration (used for GPU nodes or dedicated workloads). Node Affinity lives on Pods and attracts them to Nodes with matching labels (`requiredDuringScheduling` vs `preferredDuringScheduling`).
cards.typical_use: Controlling workload placement on heterogeneous node pools.
pitfalls: Tolerations allow a Pod to be scheduled onto a tainted node, they don't guarantee it will go there—combine with Node Affinity to isolate workloads.

cards.title: Q: What is the difference between a Service and an Ingress (or Gateway API)?
cards.question: Q: What is the difference between a Service and an Ingress (or Gateway API)?
cards.answer_30s: A: A Service provides stable L4 TCP/UDP load balancing inside/into the cluster. An Ingress (or newer Gateway API) operates at L7 HTTP/HTTPS, providing host/path routing, TLS termination, rate limiting, and virtual hosting backed by a controller (NGINX, Envoy, AWS ALB).
pitfalls: Note that Gateway API is the modern successor to Ingress with role-oriented HTTPRoute resources.

cards.title: Q: How do you achieve zero-downtime deployments and safe rollbacks?
cards.question: Q: How do you achieve zero-downtime deployments and safe rollbacks?
cards.answer_30s: A: Configure Readiness probes, `maxUnavailable: 0` with `maxSurge: 25%`, a PodDisruptionBudget, a `preStop` sleep hook, and graceful SIGTERM handling inside the app. Keep `revisionHistoryLimit` so `kubectl rollout undo` reverts instantaneously if metrics degrade.

code.body:
strategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate:
    maxSurge: 1
    maxUnavailable: 0

pitfalls: Mention canary/blue-green rollouts with Argo Rollouts or Flagger for automated metric-based promotion.

cards.title: Q: How does Kubernetes DNS and Pod-to-Pod networking work?
cards.question: Q: How does Kubernetes DNS and Pod-to-Pod networking work?
cards.answer_30s: A: Every Pod gets its own unique IP from the CNI plugin (Calico, Cilium, VPC CNI) and can reach any other Pod IP without NAT. CoreDNS resolves Service names (`svc.namespace.svc.cluster.local`) to ClusterIPs, which kube-proxy (or eBPF in Cilium) load-balances to healthy Pod endpoints.
cards.typical_use: Debugging microservice DNS and connectivity issues.
pitfalls: Mention `ndots:5` in `/etc/resolv.conf` can cause extra DNS lookups for external domains unless trailing dots or `ndots:2` are configured.
